title: Emotion-Aware Interfaces: Bridging Human and Intelligent Machines.
abstract: Emotions are fundamental to human communication and play a critical role in shaping interactions. As Artificial Intelligence advances, there is a growing demand for systems that can not only process information but also understand and respond to human emotions. Emotion-aware interfaces represent an essential step toward this goal, enabling machines to recognize users' affective states and adapt their responses in more natural and meaningful ways.

title: IMU2IMG: IMU in the Language of Vision Foundation Models.
abstract: Motivated by the growing interest in foundation models across domains such as vision and language, this study aims to explore their potential in the field of human locomotion recognition using wearable sensor data. In response to Task 1 of Sussex-Huawei Locomotion-Transportation (SHL) recognition challenge 2025, which focuses on the foundation model based user-independent activity recognition with inertial signals, our team 'HELP' proposes IMU2IMG, an algorithmic pipeline that leverages a vision foundation model for prediction. Specifically, our method transforms multimodal inertial data into RGB images, enabling explicit alignment between sensor representations and visual tokens. Through extensive experiments, we compare IMU2IMG with conventional machine learning, deep learning, and recent foundation model-based baselines. Our results demonstrate superior performance and offer insights on how sensor-to-vision mappings can support robust and interpretable human activity recognition.

title: Earable-based Continuous Blood Pressure Monitoring via a Single-Point Flexible Sensor.
abstract: Non-invasive continuous blood pressure (BP) monitoring is essential for early diagnosis and management of cardiovascular diseases in daily lives. In this work, we present an earable system that enables continuous blood pressure monitoring using a single-point flexible sensor. Leveraging the anatomical advantages of the ear region, our design integrates a soft, skin-conformal in-ear flexible sensor capable of capturing subtle arterial pulsations with high fidelity. We propose a lightweight signal processing pipeline to extract pulse wave features and estimate both systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) via a data-driven estimation model. Experimental evaluations on 20 human subjects demonstrate that our system can estimate BP with an estimation error of 1.62±3.37 mmHg for SBP and 0.19±2.84 mmHg for DBP, respectively, which fall well within the AAMI thresholds.

title: Foundation Models to Tackle Activity Recognition in Unknown Domain: Sussex-Huawei Locomotion Challenge 2025 Task 2.
abstract: This summary paper provides an overview of Task 2 from the Sussex-Huawei Locomotion Challenge. In this task, the specific category of human activity recognition was intentionally undisclosed to participants. Under these conditions, teams were expected to develop classifiers—potentially utilizing foundation models—trained on publicly available datasets, with the objective of generalizing to an unseen test set provided by the organizers. The ranking criterion was the F1 score. This paper presents a comparative analysis of the methodologies employed by participants. Additionally, it reports on further experiments conducted by the organizers using the foundation models MOMENT and Chronos.

title: Let Your Car Listen to Your Respiration Contactlessly with Ubiquitous Acoustic Signals.
abstract: Harnessing ubiquitous acoustic signals with capability of contactless respiration detection has the potential to revolutionize lots of intelligent applications. Existing work mainly employs inaudible acoustic signals to detect human respiration. To the best of our knowledge, there is a lack of public datasets due to the uniqueness of such signals. In this paper, we leverage commercial acoustic devices in cars to collect 30.79h respiration data from 23 participants and 30.98h background noise data in various scenarios over six months. An SNR enhancement pipeline is proposed to increase the SNR of data so that the neural network can capture the fine-grained respiration features. Additionally, a data augmentation pipeline is designed to enhance the diversity of the data and improve the generalization ability. Finally, we employ the proposed pipelines to train CNN-based models to detect respiration. Extensive experiments demonstrate our system can achieve a recall rate of up to 97% while maintaining a false positive rate lower than 1.11%.

title: Gesture-Based Robot Control Integrating Mm-wave Radar and Behavior Trees.
abstract: As robots become increasingly prevalent in both homes and industrial settings, the demand for intuitive and efficient human-machine interaction continues to rise. Gesture recognition offers an intuitive control method that does not require physical contact with devices and can be implemented using various sensing technologies. Wireless solutions are particularly flexible and minimally invasive. While camera-based vision systems are commonly used, they often raise privacy concerns and can struggle in complex or poorly lit environments. In contrast, radar sensing preserves privacy, is robust to occlusions and lighting, and provides rich spatial data such as distance, relative velocity, and angle. We present a gesture-controlled robotic arm using mm-wave radar for reliable, contactless motion recognition. Nine gestures are recognized and mapped to real-time commands with precision. Case studies are conducted to demonstrate the system practicality, performance and reliability for gesture-based robotic manipulation. Unlike prior work that treats gesture recognition and robotic control separately, our system unifies both into a real-time pipeline for seamless, contactless human-robot interaction.

title: BodySys 2025: The 11th Workshop on Body-Centric Computing Systems.
abstract: The 11th Workshop on Body-Centric Computing Systems (BodySys 2025) aims to advance the discussion and innovation around wearable and body-centric technologies for mobile and ubiquitous computing. Building upon a decade of successful workshops, BodySys fosters interdisciplinary dialogue among researchers and practitioners across sensing, communication, AI, health, and human-in-the-loop systems. The 2025 edition will feature keynote talks and ten technical presentations, addressing emerging topics such as implantables, intra-body communication, smart fabrics, and AI-powered wearable computing. The hybrid format encourages broad global participation and positions BodySys as a catalyst for shaping the future of human-centered mobile systems.

title: OpenBrush: An Open-Source Manual Toothbrush for Force and Motion Sensing.
abstract: Toothbrushing force and duration are both critical to effective oral hygiene, yet manual toothbrushes, the most widely used globally, lack sensing capabilities for either. We present OpenBrush, a fully open-source, force-and-motion-aware manual toothbrush that integrates a load cell in the brush neck and an inertial measurement unit (IMU) in the handle. These sensors are connected to a Raspberry Pi Pico microcontroller for onboard processing and data logging. OpenBrush enables measurement of applied brushing force and motion dynamics, offering a low-cost platform for real-time feedback, brushing behavior research, and intelligent oral care applications. We describe the mechanical and electrical design of the system and evaluate its sensing fidelity through both controlled experiments and naturalistic brushing trials. Preliminary data demonstrate the system's ability to capture fine-grained variations in force and motion. By open-sourcing the hardware and software, OpenBrush aims to empower manual toothbrush users with accessible technology to improve brushing habits, while also contributing a reproducible foundation for the research community to advance studies in oral health sensing and human–toothbrush interaction.

title: Enhancing Situational Awareness in Hearing-Impaired Drivers: A Non-Contact Alert System Using Air-Based Tactile Stimulus.
abstract: Driving presents unique challenges for hearing-impaired individuals, who often miss critical auditory cues and struggle with situational awareness. Most existing assistive systems rely on visual alerts or contact-based tactile feedback. However, visual warnings may distract drivers from the road, and contact-based tactile stimuli lack sufficient spatial resolution and flexibility. In this paper, we propose a non-contact air-based tactile feedback system comprising: (1) a low-cost air-based actuator and (2) a systematic mapping between 16 expressive tactile patterns and driving events tailored to the hearing-impaired context. A driving simulator study with five hearing-impaired participants validated the system's effectiveness: 11 out of 16 stimulus-event mappings achieved over 70% user agreement (i.e., the proportion of participant responses that aligned with the intended mapping exceeded 70%), confirming both perceptual clarity and intuitive design. These results demonstrate the potential of air-based tactile feedback to enhance situational awareness and driving safety for hearing-impaired drivers.

title: iVAS: An Intelligent Visual Development Assessment System for Infants and Toddlers.
abstract: Assessing the visual development of infants and toddlers is crucial for the early recognition of ocular abnormalities. However, traditional methods are inefficient, reliant on specialist clinicians, and necessitate professional clinical equipment. Although recent AI-driven mobile applications have improved accessibility, a gap persists for a system that integrates comprehensive, multidimensional analysis with low-cost, longitudinal monitoring. We introduce the Intelligent Visual Development Assessment System for Infants and Toddlers (iVAS), designed to operate on commercially available tablets for non-invasive, objective, and multimodal assessment. iVAS employs a novel paradigm, utilizing visual stimuli presented on the tablet's screen to elicit visual and motor responses from the infant, which are then recorded by the device's built-in sensors, including its camera, microphone, and IMU. The system's pipeline architecture leverages state-of-the-art deep learning models to extract a rich set of low-level and high-level features. By quantifying developmental metrics such as gaze, smooth pursuit, and saccade, iVAS provides a holistic evaluation of visual function. Our work aims to significantly lower the barrier for large-scale ophthalmic screening, creating a powerful tool for both parents and clinicians to track visual development and enable timely intervention.

title: MagiaSVS: Singing Voice Synthesis with Lyrics and Pitch Guidance via a Unified-Modal Large Language Model.
abstract: The rise of large language models has created new frontiers for personalized content creation, a key aspect of ubiquitous interaction. In this paper, we explore their application to Singing Voice Synthesis, a challenging task requiring the alignment of linguistic, melodic, and acoustic information. We introduce MagiaSVS, a novel framework that re-frames SVS as a unified language modeling problem. Our key contribution is an architecture that leverages a pre-trained LLM (Qwen3) and a hierarchical neural audio codec (DAC) to model multimodal inputs within a single, shared embedding space. By projecting lyrics text tokens, pitch tokens, and disentangled audio tokens (semantic and acoustic) into this unified space, MagiaSVS enables the LLM to directly learn the intricate relationships between lyrics, melody, and vocal timbre. We utilize a two-stage training strategy, involving modality-adaptive pre-training and cross-modal fine-tuning, to effectively adapt the LLM to the SVS task. We also explore the potential for MagiaSVS in wearable applications and its interplay with acoustic sensing, which could inform the future development of interactive audio experiences. Future work will focus on enhancing the performance and expanding the capabilities of MagiaSVS including its potential in wearable applications.

title: Blue Mondays and Happy Meals: Investigating the Impact of Contextual Factors on Mood States.
abstract: Mood plays a critical role in shaping cognition, memory, and well-being. While it is generally stable, it evolves gradually over time, ''emotion inertia'' phenomenon. Mood is also influenced by contextual factors, e.g., time, day, place, activity, and social context. In this study, we leverage the unique opportunity provided by the longitudinal and rich DiversityOne dataset, which includes self-reported mood and contextual information alongside smartphone sensor data collected from 782 users across eight countries over four weeks. We investigate temporal mood patterns and their associations with contextual information. Our experimental results provide quantitative evidence for the presence of the emotion inertia. Also, our findings confirm that the associations between mood and contextual factors, e.g., mood tends to be high around periods associated with meals (''Happy Meals''), and lower at the beginning of the week (''Blue Mondays''). Nevertheless, we observe cross-cultural variability in such associations. Finally, we show that integrating contextual features with mobility metrics derived from location sensor significantly enhances mood recognition performance with respect to using either feature set alone by up to six percentage points and achieving 74% balanced accuracy. These results highlight the promise of context-aware, passive sensing systems for end-to-end mood recognition with minimal reliance on self-reports.

title: Ensemble of Foundation Models for Sensor-Based Locomotion and Transportation Mode Recognition.
abstract: The UT-IR team presents an end-to-end pipeline for Task 1 of the SHL 2025 recognition challenge, which aims to recognize eight modes of transportation from smartphone inertial data. We exploit the complementary inductive biases of three large foundation models - BIOT, CBraMod, and MOMENT - to extract rich time-series representations. Their frozen embeddings are unified through a lightweight three-layer MLP that learns to arbitrate among the experts. Evaluated on the modified validation set, the ensemble attains 92.37% accuracy and a 92.44% Weighted-F1 score, surpassing the strongest single backbone by 2.71 pp. Detailed agreement analysis shows that BIOT and CBraMod provide a robust baseline for stationary and mixed-motion activities, while MOMENT contributes decisive cues for highly dynamic classes; their fusion markedly reduces confusion between visually similar transportation modes. These findings demonstrate that the ensemble of pre-trained time-series transformers is a practical and effective path to state-of-the-art, real-world activity recognition.

title: Characterising Parkinson's Disease-like Walking Using Wrist-worn Accelerometers.
abstract: Changes in walking patterns are a well-known symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD), traditionally assessed through clinical observation. Advances in wearable technology and machine learning (ML) offer new opportunities for early detection, disease monitoring, and treatment evaluation.

title: Integrating Conversational Assistants with Smart Mirrors for Mental Health Assessment.
abstract: The global aging trend demands innovative solutions to support older adults in maintaining emotional well-being and independent living. Depression and anxiety remain underdiagnosed in this population due to social stigma and lack of regular screening. To address this gap, we propose ESPELHAR, a smart mirror-based conversational assistant for continued mental health assessment at home. Building upon clinically validated instruments, namely the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and General Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), our approach reimagines these tools as daily micro-assessments embedded into natural conversation. The assistant dynamically adapts the questions, scores responses through an inverted cumulative method, and maintains a temporal emotional profile to detect trends and worsening symptoms. This contribution presents the definition of Personas and Scenarios that guided system requirements, a detailed proposal for the mood assessment method, and the implementation of an initial system prototype. By grounding daily mood monitoring in robust psychometrics and more natural interaction, our approach bridges the gap between traditional clinical screening and real-world smart environments. Overall, we believe this work has the potential to support proactive mental health care at home.

title: SocialPulse: An On-Smartwatch System for Detecting Real-World Social Interactions.
abstract: Social interactions are a fundamental part of daily life and play a critical role in well-being. As emerging technologies offer opportunities to unobtrusively monitor behavior, there is growing interest in using them to better understand social experiences. However, automatically detecting interactions, particularly via wearable devices, remains underexplored. Existing systems are often limited to controlled environments, constrained to in-person interactions, and rely on rigid assumptions such as the presence of two speakers within a fixed time window. These limitations reduce their generalizability to capture diverse real-world interactions. To address these challenges, we developed a real-time, on-watch system capable of detecting both in-person and virtual interactions. The system leverages transfer learning to detect foreground speech (FS) and infers interaction boundaries based upon FS and conversational cues like whispering. In a real-world evaluation involving 11 participants over a total of 38 days (Mean = 3.45 days, SD = 2.73), the system achieved an interaction detection accuracy of 73.18%. Follow-up with six participants indicated perfect recall for detecting interactions. These preliminary findings demonstrate the potential of our system to capture interactions in daily life, providing a foundation for applications such as personalized interventions targeting social anxiety.

title: Memory-Augmented LLMs for Sustainable Urban Energy Management via Weather-Energy Pattern Learning.
abstract: This paper presents a novel dual-memory Large Language Model (LLM) architecture for sustainable urban energy management. Inspired by hippocampal-neocortical interactions, the approach integrates fast learning with long-term memory consolidation to capture weather-energy correlations. The LLM processes meteorological data through natural language interfaces, enabling semantic understanding of weather patterns. Evaluated across European cities using Open-Meteo and ENTSO-E data, the dual-memory LLM achieves 60-85% MAPE improvements over LSTM baselines (2.02-6.13% vs 10.46-17.98%), with cost savings averaging €152M per city. title: Exploring Generalist Foundation Models for Time Series of Electrodermal Activity Data.
abstract: Wearable devices increasingly incorporate physiological sensors, including electrodermal activity (EDA), to monitor human states. EDA measures skin conductance changes reflecting arousal in the Autonomic Nervous System, making it valuable for stress monitoring, cognitive load assessment, and health-related tasks. However, practical challenges such as sensor placement, physiological variability, and data availability impact EDA-based applications. Recently, foundation models, trained through self-supervision on diverse datasets, have shown the potential to generalize across domains, addressing data scarcity and variability, making them compelling for EDA. We explore the applicability of four time series foundation models (Chronos, MOMENT, TSMixer, Mantis), applied to EDA data from four datasets (USILaughs, SEED, APsync, BiHeartS). We compare the performance of features from the foundation models against traditional handcrafted features for tasks including cognitive load, engagement, and sleep/wake classification. Our experiments indicate that using features from the Chronos and Mantis foundation models leads to similar performance as handcrafted features across most tasks, with other models also not surpassing the traditional approach. These results highlight the potential yet underscore the necessity of developing specialized EDA foundation models. Future research should address challenges of dataset availability and variability to fully exploit the capabilities of foundation models for EDA-based sensing.

title: Mitigating Interpersonal Variability in Machine Learning Models for Human Behavior Monitoring.
abstract: Machine learning models for human behavior monitoring typically rely on population-level data, assuming that physiological patterns generalize well across individuals. However, this assumption often fails due to interpersonal variability — differences in individuals' physiological responses and subjective interpretations influenced by personal, cultural, and psychological factors. This research first investigates how such variability impacts model performance in two scenarios: sleep monitoring, where label variability arises because individuals assign different subjective ratings to similar physiological patterns, and transport mode recognition, where signal variability occurs as individuals exhibit distinct sensor signals for the same activity. Our empirical findings show that population models struggle to generalize, especially in tasks involving subjective assessments. To overcome these challenges, we firstly propose generative modeling techniques to augment limited user-specific data, and secondly introduce a clustering-based strategy that enables scalable personalization by grouping users according to both physiological signal patterns and labeling behavior.

title: Robust PPG Authentication: The Role of Temporal, Individual, and State Variability.
abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG), a signal tracking blood volume changes, encodes user-specific patterns for unobtrusive authentication. This study investigates three real-world factors that affect the reliability of PPG-based authentication: temporal variability (time elapsed between training and test), user-specific variability (differences in individual identifiability), and state-dependent variability (changes in states such as stress or mood). We use the LAUREATE dataset, which includes longitudinal PPG signals and self-reported states (e.g., stress, happiness, sleep quality) from 44 participants over 13 weeks. We train a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN) to identify users from 180-second PPG segments. Results show no systematic decline in performance due to temporal variability, but notable individual and daily fluctuations. Some users are consistently identified with high accuracy, while others show more variable performance, indicating identifiability varies across individuals. Most notably, the performance of the model improves when trained on data matching the test-state value, yielding up to 0.3 higher Matthews Correlation Coefficient for individual states and 0.11–0.2 improvement when states are grouped using the PANAVA-KS scale. These findings suggest that state-dependent variability, rather than time, is the primary limitation of biometric authentication systems. Robust authentication systems should incorporate multi-state training and context-aware modeling to ensure consistent performance in real-world settings.

title: Identifying Routine from Sequences of Activities of Daily Living in Smart-homes.
abstract: Routine identification in smart homes is a challenging task with applications in health monitoring, adaptive home automation, and supporting rehabilitation and recovery efforts. In this study, we focus on identifying routines by comparing the performance of WaveNet, and GPT with MLP model on two datasets: Orange4Home and Aruba. We examine how sequence length, embedding size, and contextual features (such as time, location and day-of-week) affect model performance. Our results show that moderate sequence lengths and smaller embedding improve generalization, and the impact of added context varies by models and datasets. While GPT outperforms other models in next-activity prediction— as expected given its contextual modeling capabilities— MLP shows superior performance in reconstructing full-day sequences without prompts. These findings highlight the importance of choosing the right model and representation for accurate routine identification in smart home systems.

title: A Visual Context Aware Solution for Protecting Mobile Users from Visual Privacy Attacks.
abstract: With the increasing use of mobile devices in public spaces, users are becoming increasingly vulnerable to visual privacy attacks, commonly known as shoulder surfing. These attacks enable bystanders to visually extract sensitive information from screens without authorization. In this work, we introduce a novel context-aware framework that leverages mobile device camera sensors and bystander positions to detect and prevent visual privacy attacks. Specifically, we present: a reactive system that detects nearby intruders using the front-facing camera and alerts users in real-time, and a proactive text reader that dynamically adjusts content visibility to thwart unauthorized viewing. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates the robustness of our system in varied real-world scenarios. This work lays the groundwork for intelligent, user-friendly visual privacy protection on mobile platforms.

title: Privacy-Preserving Real-Time Human Activity Recognition Using On-Device Small Language Models.
abstract: Personal well-being monitoring requires sophisticated contextual reasoning, creating a fundamental tension: cloud-based models violate user privacy, while privacy-preserving methods lack semantic understanding. We approach this challenge with ODCSIS (On-Device Contextual Sensing and Inference System), which deploys Small Language Models (SLMs) for end-to-end behavioral analysis entirely on-device, ensuring complete data sovereignty. Our preliminary evaluation of the Gemma 3n E4B and E2B models reveals an unexpected finding: in our experiments, the smaller E2B model demonstrated more stable performance across different few-shot configurations, while the larger E4B model exhibited degradation with additional examples. Our work provides both a complete system architecture and initial empirical evidence suggesting that model stability may be more important than scale for real-world behavioral sensing applications.

title: Health Assistants for Everyday Care: Reliable Human?AI Collaboration under Imperfect Sensing.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare has excelled in clinical tasks such as diagnostics and patient monitoring. Yet, it still falls short in meeting the daily needs of patients with chronic conditions and cognitive impairments, particularly in providing in-situ assistance for everyday care. My research aims to develop intelligent health assistants that go beyond reactive alerts and passive monitoring to provide proactive, context-aware interventions to support it. Key contributions include advancing sensing technologies to capture richer, real-world contextual data and designing assistive systems that support both patients and caregivers and adapt through daily interactions. I evaluate these systems in diverse domains, including post-operative skin cancer care, dementia support, and child hyperactivity management. Through these field deployments, my thesis aims to articulate design strategies for effective human-AI collaboration in the presence of sensing uncertainty, ultimately promoting positive behavior change and fostering greater autonomy in everyday care.

title: Toward a Testbed for the Internet of Underwater Things: Challenges and Considerations.
abstract: The Internet of Underwater Things (IoUT) is an emerging approach composed of a network of underwater devices, such as sensors, vehicles, and communication nodes, that collaboratively collect, transmit, and analyze data for applications such as ocean monitoring, underwater exploration, and defense. The vision of IoUT includes significant challenges for communication due to signal attenuation, multipath interference, and limited bandwidth. This paper presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of a basic underwater acoustic communication system. One of the purposes of this paper was to explore how components coming from the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem can be integrated into the IoUT paradigm. Therefore, we compare a microcontroller with a signal generator for the signal generation process to evaluate performance trade-offs. Performance was assessed across configurations in a pool environment. Key findings include reliable communication at 300 bps up to 6 meters (BER <10% with Hamming encoding) and reliable performance up to 1000 bps at 1 meter (BER ≈ 1%) using a microcontroller instead of a signal generator. This paper demonstrates the first steps to build a testbed to evaluate IoUT solutions that will offer practical insights into the challenges and performance factors of simple underwater acoustic communication.

title: Tracking Radial Artery Dynamics Using Brightness-Mode Ultrasound and Video Analysis.
abstract: Cardiovascular disease is an important concern and the evaluation of vascular health is a key element for early detection. However, continuous non-invasive measurement of vascular health is limited to clinical settings while wearable health sensing devices are lacking vascular health detection. To achieve such wearable continuous cardiovascular health measurement, better understanding about physical properties of the vascular system are needed. Towards the development of wearable continuous cardiovascular health monitoring, we developed, verified, and validated an algorithm to estimate the dynamic radius of the radial artery and estimated the arterial pulsation from brightness-mode ultrasound imaging. The algorithm was implemented using Python and MATLAB®. The algorithm was tested using a simulation environment, as well as ultrasound imaging together with continuous non-invasive arterial pressure monitoring from participants. The radial artery size and distance from surface measured was >90% accurate. We report an informative summary from 6 participants. The radial artery radius change over time was used to estimate heart-beat rate, and showed reasonable accuracy for 5 out of 6 participants.

title: Smart Textiles, HCI and User's Dignity.
abstract: Smart textile-based sensors and actuators represent a paradigm shift in wearable technology, seamlessly integrating sensing capabilities into everyday fabrics while maintaining comfort and wearability. These advanced materials enable medical-grade physiological monitoring (e.g., heart rate, respiration, muscle activity) and intuitive human-computer interaction (HCI), addressing limitations of traditional rigid electronic sensors in comfort, discretion, and long-term usability. This review explores how smart textiles align with future HCI goals—intuitive design, multimodal interaction, contextual understanding, metaphorical communication, and personalization—while highlighting applications in healthcare, sports science, industrial safety, and consumer electronics. We also discuss current research challenges, interdisciplinary gaps, and user's dignity, supported by recent advancements from our decade-long research in flexible sensing technologies.

title: Head Movement-Based Visual Distraction Detection in Cyclists with Earables.
abstract: Visual distractions among cyclists significantly reduce their situational awareness, increasing the likelihood of accidents. This study introduces the use of an open-source OpenEarable device, equipped with onboard inertial measurement units (IMU), as an easy and non-invasive way to detect visual distractions by measuring head movements linked to such behaviors. Head movement data from 20 participants were collected during natural cycling situations using earable IMU sensors. Both classical machine learning and deep learning techniques are employed to analyze the data to detect visual distractions. Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) achieve weighted F1 scores of 0.85 and 0.87, and Cohen's Kappa scores of 0.74 and 0.59, respectively. These findings highlight the potential of earable devices in real-time distraction detection and establish a foundation for future wearable safety systems for cyclists.

title: Exploring Smartphone-based Spectrophotometry for Vitamin B12 Quantification.
abstract: Imbalanced nutrition is a global health issue with significant downstream effects. Existing nutrient assessment methods face several limitations, with accessibility being a major concern. In this study, we step towards developing technology for measuring nutrient status in an accessible way. We prototyped a smartphone-based spectrophotometer and tested its feasibility for measuring the absorbance spectra of vitamin B12 in a solution. We investigated the effects of various light sources and reference spectra calculation methods on smartphone-based spectrophotometry. To further validate our prototype, we compared the device to a benchtop laboratory spectrophotometer. Leveraging the Beer-Lambert Law, our prototype quantified the amount of vitamin B12 in a solution with an accuracy of up to 91.3%. Our work provides initial evidence for the utility of smartphone-based spectrophotometry as an accessible method to identify and quantify nutrients, paving the way for future developments aimed at other nutrients or in-body assessment.

title: A Hybrid Generative Model based on Diffusion and Graphs for Cross-Correlated Synthetic Multivariate Time Series Data.
abstract: The prediction of missing sensor data in human activity recognition is an active field of research that is being targeted with generative models for synthetic data generation. In contrast to most previous approaches, which focus on extrapolation or prediction of data samples of a particular sensor, we target the generation of data for new sensor locations or modalities, i.e., different body locations or sensor modalities for which data had not been recorded in the first place. This is possible due to inherent correlations in the motion of human body parts. Particularly, from a larger body of training data, comprising diverse kinds of sensor body locations and modalities, we aim to learn correlations between body parts and sensor modalities, which are used to train a generative model to predict from existing sensor data of an individual subject, sensor modalities at different body locations. We also evaluate existing approaches proposed in the literature for their suitability in this scenario. This paper proposes a hybrid machine learning model based on diffusion and graph neural networks.

title: Optimized Personnel Tracking via Theoretical-Actual Acoustic Matching and Joint Active-Passive Constraint.
abstract: Indoor personnel tracking plays a vital role in smart home applications such as security monitoring, elderly care, and appliance control. While passive acoustic localization offers privacy-preserving and non-invasive tracking by estimating the angle-of-arrival (AoA) of sound, it struggles in complex environments with low signal-to-noise ratios and multiple sound sources. Active acoustic methods improve robustness but often suffer from limited deployment flexibility and high computational cost. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel acoustic signal fusion solution via utilizing audio system microphones, fully integrating active and passive acoustic signals. Our approach corrects angular prediction biases in passive sensing and incorporates beamforming-based ranging for accurate distance estimation. By comparing theoretical sampling matrices with real-time data and applying conjugate multiplication, we jointly optimize angle and range measurements. A fusion model further enhances overall tracking accuracy. Extensive experiments show that the proposed method achieves a tracking range of 5.2~m, reduces the median position error to under 11~cm, and improves angular accuracy compared to both passive-only and active-only baselines.

title: Harnessing Unstable Underground Wind for Passive LoRa-Based Human Activity Detection in Coal Mines.
abstract: Human activity detection in underground coal mines is challenged by harsh environments and limited energy availability. This study presents a passive sensing system that harnesses unstable underground wind, induced by mine ventilation, to power LoRa-based communication nodes without relying on external power supplies. To mitigate signal intermittency caused by fluctuating wind energy, a Mean Intermittent Amplitude Ratio (MIAR) algorithm is proposed for extracting robust activity features under high interference. The system incorporates adaptive filtering and sliding window techniques to isolate valid signal segments, enabling reliable personnel detection and gesture recognition. Experimental results show that the Random Forest model achieves robust detection performance, while the ResNet model accurately classifies four representative gestures. The solution demonstrates high deployment flexibility, strong resilience to interference, and full energy autonomy, offering a viable approach for non-contact, battery-free sensing in blind zones and disaster-prone areas of underground coal mines.

title: The CARP Mobile Sensing Framework - Demonstration.
abstract: Mobile sensing - i.e., the ability to unobtrusively collect sensor data from built-in phones and attached wearable sensors - is a core research topic in Ubicomp. Here, we present a demonstration of the CARP Mobile Sensing (CAMS) framework, a modern cross-platform (Android / iOS) software architecture providing a reactive and unified programming model that emphasizes extensibility, maintainability, and adaptability. CAMS has evolved since 2018, released in several versions, has been used in implementing a wide number of mobile health (mHealth) applications, and is well-documented. We demonstrate the software design, the programming model, documentation, and extensibility of CAMS.

title: A Proposal for a Multimodal Interactive Platform for Data Collection in Autism Play-Based Therapy Sessions.
abstract: We present the prototype of a novel multimodal platform for behavioural data acquisition, designed to support therapists during play-based sessions with children with Autism Spectrum Conditions (ASC). Play-based therapy sessions can offer therapists valuable insights that support both diagnostic assessment and therapeutic decision-making. Since these type of insights come from several interactions between the therapists, the child and the environment; therapists could require automated multimodal systems that can capture and retain behavioural data beyond what can be observed through experience. The proposed system integrates four components: Echo, a smart toy capable to automatically recognize different symbolic play activities when a child plays with it; 2 Camera Glasses, worn by two therapists, to record Video & Audio data from two different viewpoints; A Computer Vision algorithm to detect the gaze between the child and one of the therapist; and a Platform Application that allow to examine synchronized data logging to reconstruct the interaction between the child, the toy and the therapist within the session. The proposed environment is potentially a a powerful time-saving data collection instrument for therapists and enables improved analysis to support research on social participation in ASC treatment.

title: Harnessing Edge Computing and Artificial Intelligence for Real-Time Video Analytics in Disaster Management.
abstract: The confluence of the Internet of Things (IoT), edge computing, and artificial intelligence (AI) represents a transformative approach to addressing critical challenges in disaster management through real-time video analytics. The latency inherent in cloud-based processing of large-scale video streams fails to meet the stringent response time requirements essential for effective emergency response, as delays of even a few seconds can significantly impact rescue outcomes. This paper presents RescueAll, an application that leverages edge computing, 5G communication, and AI to enhance rescue team coordination during disasters. With AI-driven real-time video analytics and a low-latency edge-based architecture, RescueAll facilitates automatic detection and classification of critical events and maintains operational continuity even in areas with compromised network connectivity. These features enable emergency responders to access critical situational awareness capabilities under challenging conditions, thereby enhancing the efficiency, coordination, and safety of disaster response efforts.

title: Digitally Induced Altered States as Facilitators of the Future Augmented Human Sensorium: Analysis of Science Fiction Representations.
abstract: This work analyses science fiction narratives for the intersections between the evolution of sensory augmentation technologies and altered states of consciousness as means of adaptation to this evolution. It identifies four types of sensorium manipulation, namely replacement, expansion, sharing and suppression, with each relating to unique cognitive shifts. Their representations in science fiction suggest that at least three of them can benefit from the facilitation of these shifts through appropriate types of digitally induced altered states of consciousness.

title: WiFi-Based People Counting Using Beam-Steerable Antennas: A Test-bed Study.
abstract: RF sensing is an emerging technology paradigm that repurposes existing wireless communication networks, such as WiFi, for imaging and computer vision applications, namely ambient and human sensing. Recent research has demonstrated that RF holography techniques can surpass human vision capabilities in several tasks such as identifying and resolving individuals within dense crowds, interpreting gestures and emotions, and capturing images through walls. The paper explores the use of pattern-reconfigurable antenna devices with unmodified WiFi signals for indoor people discrimination, namely counting the number of people co-present in the space. We discuss signal modeling, integration of beam-steering technology, and adaptation for this purpose. Initial case studies and performance analyses within a test-house environment are also presented.

title: Utilizing Speech as a Biosignal for Monitoring Respiratory Health and Beyond.
abstract: Speech arises from the complex coordination of respiratory, neurological, cardiovascular, and muscular systems, making it a rich yet underutilized biosignal for health monitoring. This research explores the use of speech captured via mobile and wearable devices to assess and monitor respiratory health, with a focus on individuals with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It introduces methods for passive, continuous symptom monitoring using natural speech and explores structure-preserving speech representations to estimate lung function from acoustic features. Building on the insights from speech-based respiratory assessments, this thesis proposes a disease-agnostic speech diagnostic framework powered by self-supervised learning. By enabling low-burden, scalable assessments from natural speech, it supports equitable access to early diagnostics and personalized care across a broad spectrum of health conditions.

title: Passive Body-Area Electrostatic Field (Human Body Capacitance) for Ubiquitous Computing.
abstract: Passive body-area electrostatic field sensing, also referred to as human body capacitance (HBC), is an energy-efficient and non-intrusive sensing modality that exploits the human body's inherent electrostatic properties to perceive human behaviors. This paper presents a focused overview of passive HBC sensing, including its underlying principles, historical evolution, hardware architectures, and applications across research domains. Key challenges, such as susceptibility to environmental variation, are discussed to trigger mitigation techniques. Future research opportunities in sensor fusion and hardware enhancement are highlighted. To support continued innovation, this work provides open-source resources and aims to empower researchers and developers to leverage passive electrostatic sensing for next-generation wearable and ambient intelligence systems. https://github.com/zhaxidele/Toolkit-for-HBC-sensing.

title: DiversityOne Open Challenge: Exploring People's Everyday Life Behavior with Mobile Data.
abstract: Combining passive smartphone sensor data with self-reports enables the study of everyday life behavior. The DiversityOne dataset, recently released to the UbiComp community, overcomes the limitation of existing datasets by containing data from eight countries from both Global South and Global North, including data from 782 college students, combining the data from 26 smartphone sensors and 350K+ self-reports, and extensive demographic and psychosocial survey data from 18K college students. The richness of the dataset opens the way to investigating important problems in multiple disciplines. Existing studies that leverage the dataset have only scratched the surface of the potential research questions it can help answer. Thus, we are organizing this workshop to foster creative and multidisciplinary works on this dataset: from AI and ubiquitous and mobile computing to computational social science and design.

title: Envisioning Physical Collaboration at a Distance: Design Fiction for Hybrid Prototyping.
abstract: This workshop invites participants to explore the futures of distributed collaboration in hybrid manufacturing environments through the lens of Design Fiction. Drawing on scenarios inspired by real-life observations in university FabLabs, participants will co-create narrative prototypes in the form of quick-start guides. The workshop interweaves human and technological, tangible and digital dimensions within a postdigital perspective, aligning with the paradigm of ubiquitous learning. It seeks to interrogate the conditions that enable phygital continuity between physical co-presence and remote participation. Aimed at an interdisciplinary community, the workshop invites critical engagement with emerging uses of ubiquitous computing and wearable technologies in collaborative practices.

title: mFQS: A Multidimensional Visual Rating System.
abstract: Expressing our opinions using rating systems in everyday life is a common practice. People often need to evaluate content for research, commercial applications, and personal expression. These evaluations provide important information for organizations. The limitation of current rating systems is that they often follow ordinal scales, like the Likert Scale, or are limited to binary voting. These rating systems only work on certain interfaces, lack flexibility to engage in nuanced evaluation requests, and can suffer from cultural biases. In this work, we introduce a graphical scale, the modified four-quadrant gradient rating scale (mFQS), designed to overcome these limitations. The mFQS allows users to rate multiple aspects at the same time while providing more granular control over the rating. The preliminary results show that the study participants found the system easier to use than the Likert scale and that there was a significant advantage in obtaining nuanced ratings from Japanese participants. Future directions for this work will look at implementing these scales in public contexts.

abstract: This paper presents LODYSEI, an ongoing project aiming at generating intelligible, intuitive and easy to memorize object position descriptions in natural language for blind people. We present preliminary results concerning the development and testing of an indoor localization system using Ultra-Wideband (UWB) technology, the evaluation of a voice recognition interface and the use of the localization information by a Large Language Model (LLM) in order to generate position descriptions in French.

title: Machine Learning-Driven Forecasting of Glucose Drops in Exercise.
abstract: Managing blood glucose in daily life is crucial for individuals living with diabetes. Ensuring that intense physical activity can be performed safely, without increasing the risk of hypoglycemia, remains a significant challenge. This paper presents a data-driven approach for predicting whether a planned exercise session is likely to lead to a high glucose drop. The prediction is based not only on session characteristics such as duration and intensity but also on contextual and individual-level factors including past activity patterns, continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data, and patient-specific information such as age and health status. The goal is to support proactive self-management by providing personalized alerts and recommendations before exercise begins.

title: A Preliminary Taxonomy and Evaluation Methodology for Recursive Bioadaptive Media.
abstract: This paper examines recursive bioadaptive media as a class of perception-modulating systems that use psychophysiological and affective signals (e.g., EEG, HRV, EDA, eye tracking) to alter media parameters in real time. Unlike augmenting human sensation through prosthetic extension, these systems operate through recursive bioadaptive loops that modulate cognition, affect, and embodied experience. Drawing on interdisciplinary work across HCI, immersive media, affective computing, and critical theory, we argue that bioadaptive media constitute a form of techno-biological infrastructure that raises epistemic, aesthetic, and ethical questions. We present a preliminary work-in-progress sociotechnical taxonomy of such systems and offer a framework for assessing their implications for user experience, agency, and normative assumptions about cognition, affect, and perception.

title: WHAR Datasets: An Open Source Library for Wearable Human Activity Recognition.
abstract: The lack of standardization across Wearable Human Activity Recognition (WHAR) datasets limits reproducibility, comparability, and research efficiency. We introduce WHAR datasets, an open-source library designed to simplify WHAR data handling through a standardized data format and a configuration-driven design, enabling reproducible and computationally efficient workflows with minimal manual intervention. The library currently supports 9 widely-used datasets, integrates with PyTorch and TensorFlow, and is easily extensible to new datasets. To demonstrate its utility, we trained two state-of-the-art models, TinyHar and MLP-HAR, on the included datasets, approximately reproducing published results and validating the library's effectiveness for experimentation and benchmarking. Additionally, we evaluated preprocessing performance and observed speedups of up to 3.8× using multiprocessing. We hope this library contributes to more efficient, reproducible, and comparable WHAR research.

title: Design and Challenges of Mental Health Assessment Tools Based on Natural Language Interaction.
abstract: Mental health assessments are of central importance to individuals' well-being. Conventional assessment methodologies predominantly depend on clinical interviews and standardised self-report questionnaires. Nevertheless, the efficacy of these methodologies is frequently impeded by factors such as subjectivity, recall bias, and accessibility issues. Furthermore, concerns regarding bias and privacy may result in misreporting in data collected through self-reporting in mental health research. The present study examined the design opportunities and challenges inherent in the development of a mental health assessment tool based on natural language interaction with large language models (LLMs). An interactive prototype system was developed using conversational AI for non-invasive mental health assessment, and was evaluated through semi-structured interviews with 11 mental health professionals (six counsellors and five psychiatrists). The analysis identified key design considerations for future development, highlighting how AI-driven adaptive questioning could potentially enhance the reliability of self-reported data while identifying critical challenges, including privacy protection, algorithmic bias, and cross-cultural applicability. This study provides an empirical foundation for mental health technology innovation by demonstrating the potential and limitations of natural language interaction in mental health assessment.

title: FLUX Mouse: A Seamless High-DOF Input Device for Intuitive 3D Interaction.
abstract: Spatial controllers enable rich 3D interactions but often compromise the precision and ergonomic familiarity of traditional mice. Existing solutions typically remain specialized, forcing users to juggle multiple devices or adapt to unfamiliar form factors. We introduce the FLUX Mouse, a spatial input device that combines traditional mouse ergonomics with 3D interaction capabilities, featuring fully automatic transitions between 2D cursor control and 6 DOF spatial interaction. The FLUX Mouse integrates an optical sensor for 2D tasks with an inertial measurement unit and binocular infrared vision tracking for 3D tracking, and uses adaptive pressure sensing to balance precision and speed. Preliminary user feedback suggests intuitive usability, a manageable learning curve, and positive acceptance, indicating the potential to support psychological needs as outlined by Self-Determination Theory across diverse applications from professional modeling to immersive gaming.

title: FAME: Feature-Augmented Multi-View Ensemble Framework for Human Activity Recognition using Inertial Sensors.
abstract: This technical report presents the approach and insights of team ''Whatever'' for the 2nd Edition of the WEAR Challenge. This challenge proposes an Inertia-Based Human Activity Recognition (HAR) problem focused on identifying sports activities using data collected by wearable sensors. To address this, we propose a multi-view ensemble model considering each view as the set of symmetrically worn sensors (i.e., right/left arm). The model is composed of an early encoder that shares weights across the views, followed by two view-specific branches (wrist and legs). We further encourage similarity between symmetric sensor positions by adding a similarity component to the loss function. We enrich inputs with frequency-domain and PCA features plus data augmentation. Our evaluation revealed that frequency-domain features and channel-wise random sign-flipping data augmentation were the main drivers of generalization, mirroring patterns seen on the challenge test set. Code available on GitHub https://github.com/FranciscoCalatrava/FAME-Feature-Augmented-Multi-View-Ensemble.git.

title: Workshop on Moralizing Radio Frequency Holography for Palliative Care via Value-Sensitive Design.
abstract: Palliative care provides healthcare treatment to patients with critical and terminal medical conditions at the end of their lives. This type of care is usually provided in highly medicalised settings, given the current health provision at hospitals, depriving many patients of the possibility to spend their final moments at home with their loved ones. At home, radio frequency (RF) holography is considered a possible solution or assistant for these concerns. Radio frequency holography utilises electromagnetic waves, typically used for Wi-Fi, to gain a deeper understanding of occurrences within an environment by applying computational reasoning, such as machine learning, to visualise or label feedback. This new technology has the potential to disrupt social norms and standards and change the phenomenology of palliative care for terminal residents, healthcare professionals, and family members alike. This paper presents a methodology to apply value-sensitive design (VSD) to RF holography for palliative care to help engineers gain tools and the vocabulary to better communicate, understand, and address ethical concerns in the technologies they build.

title: Federated Learning for Human Activity Recognition with Environmental and Subject-Level Awareness.
abstract: In human activity recognition studies, the location of the sensors and environmental conditions are determined with precision during the data collection process, and this positioning can directly affect the model performance. In addition, the individual characteristics of the participants while performing the activities stand out as a separate problem element that makes the generalizability of the system difficult. In order to overcome these two problems, the federated learning method was applied in the presented study to obtain a model that adapts to different environmental conditions and has a high generalization capacity among users. Within the scope of this study, studies were carried out on two different scenarios. In these scenarios, client types were determined as environment-based and subject-based and the studies were carried out in this direction. In addition, the effect of aggregation functions on system performance was examined in these two scenarios. The experimental results show that FedAdam achieves superior performance in environment-based systems, while FedYogi achieves superior performance in subject-based systems.

title: Sensor-Specific Transformer (PatchTST) Ensembles with Test-Matched Augmentation.
abstract: We present a noise-aware, sensor-specific ensemble approach for robust human activity recognition on the 2nd WEAR Dataset Challenge. Our method leverages the PatchTST transformer architecture, training four independent models—one per inertial sensor location—on a ''tampered'' training set whose 1-second sliding windows are augmented to mimic the test-time noise. By aligning the train and test data schemas (JSON-encoded 50-sample windows) and applying randomized jitter, scaling, rotation, and channel dropout, each PatchTST model learns to generalize across real-world sensor perturbations. At inference, we compute softmax probabilities from all four sensor models on the Kaggle test set and average them to produce final labels. On the private leaderboard, this pipeline achieves a macro-F1 substantially above the baseline, demonstrating that test-matched augmentation combined with transformer-based ensembling is an effective strategy for robust HAR under noisy conditions.

title: Where Does the Noise Come From? Understanding Challenges in Enhancing the Accuracy of Learning-Based Emotion Inference for Virtual Reality Applications Using EEG Signals.
abstract: This study explored strategies to improve the quality of data collected in the training of emotion detection algorithms. A binary classification algorithm was developed to classify emotions as high or low in valence and arousal, based on EEG data recorded while participants viewed 360-degree Virtual Reality (VR) videos. Participants also self-reported their emotional responses through a VR-based interface, providing ground-truth labels for model training. Through a combination of quantitative and qualitative observations, we identified several challenges in the data collection process, including issues related to user discomfort, EEG signal consistency, and the reliability of self-reported emotions. In response, we proposed practical solutions to improve emotion inference accuracy by minimizing VR-induced discomfort, enhancing EEG data quality, and standardizing self-report procedures.

title: Beyond the Sharing of Personal Data: Design of Collaborative Chatbot-based Mobile Support Systems to Facilitate Recovery from Alcohol Use Disorder.
abstract: Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) is a chronic condition with profound negative consequences for one's health and personal relationships. In this pilot needs-finding study, we interviewed four AUD patient-family dyads to investigate the integration of chatbot technology with existing self-monitoring and social sensing tools in AUD treatment. Insights from these interviews informed the design of mobile applications aimed at promoting collaboration between patients and family companions. A chatbot-powered backend supports self-monitoring, facilitates family updates, and provides continuous guidance via a 24/7 conversational agent. Subsequent research will involve a field study to evaluate the feasibility of the system for clinical application in AUD management.

title: Exploring Singing Breath: Physiological Insights and Directions for Breath-Aware Augmentation in Mixed Reality Design.
abstract: This paper investigates singing breath, the distinctive respiratory pattern that occurs while singing a melody, as a structured and expressive form of breathing that can support breath-aware interaction. First, we conduct a user study to collect the breath dataset from 16 amateur singers using a custom wearable breath band. Next, we analyze and evaluate the multi-site respiratory data across four conditions (rest, deep, pitch, and song breath). The initial results show that pitch tasks elicit stronger ribcage expansion while song tasks naturally encourage abdominal engagement. Building on these insights, we design a Mixed Reality (MR) system that visualizes real-time breath using particle-based feedback to enhance somatic awareness. We position singing breath as an engaging and embodied alternative to conventional breathing training and propose directions for breath-aware augmentation that combine biosensing, MR, and affective self-regulation.

title: Parametric Model of Differential SAW Pressure Sensor: Enabling Rapid Performance Evaluation and Optimization Design.
abstract: Differential Surface Acoustic Wave (SAW) pressure sensors are widely used across various fields. To enable faster and more accurate performance evaluations, we developed a parametric model. This model divides the interdigital transducer (IDT) structure into several microelements and combines it with a small deflection deformation model of the diaphragm, allowing for rapid calculation of sensor performance parameters under different structures. Comparisons with existing experimental results show that the model achieves an accuracy of over 80%. Owing to its computational speed, we applied the model to uncertainty analysis and structural optimization. The results indicate that the width of the IDT has the greatest impact on sensitivity uncertainty. After optimization, the sensitivity increased by a factor of 2.18, and the uncertainty decreased to 60.5% of the original.

Through multi-phase evaluations with novice and expert singers, we demonstrate how physiological feedback enhances vocal control, reveals skill differences, and informs predictive models for real-time guidance. Our findings highlight the potential of muscle-acoustic sensing in embodied vocal learning.

title: Introduction of the VCSD Dataset: A Vocal Cords Dataset Using EMG and Ultrasonography for Singing Pitch Skill Recognition.
abstract: We present the Vocal Cords Sensing Dataset (VCSD), a multimodal dataset for analyzing singing pitch skills using surface electromyography (EMG) and ultrasonography (UI). The dataset includes over three hours of recordings from 16 participants with varied singing experience, capturing EMG signals and ultrasound vocal fold motion. VCSD supports the recognition of vocal pitch control and muscle coordination during the pitch singing. Initial analysis shows significant differences in EMG stability and vocal fold dynamics between novice and expert singers. This dataset enables future research in vocal training, physiological sensing, and interactive feedback design.

title: Nexa: A Context-Aware Assistant for Service Recommendation on Smartphones.
abstract: Smartphone services are growing rapidly in number and complexity, making traditional graphical user interfaces increasingly inefficient for service access. To improve accessibility, we propose Nexa, a unified, self-evolving context-aware assistant that integrates multimodal user input (such as voice commands, camera input, screen content and motion gestures) and contextual information (such as time, location, network and notification) to recommend and execute smartphone services. For service recommendation, the assistant employs a dual-layered prediction module: a rule-based System 1 for fast matching, complemented by an LLM-based System 2 that performs reasoning when no rules apply. The system continuously learns from user interactions; when recommendations fail, it logs the user's subsequent GUI interactions and updates its prediction model by analyzing causal relationships among multimodal inputs, context, and the final chosen service. Additionally, macro scripts are extracted from logged GUI traces and added to the service list. We implement a prototype on Android with a cloud backend. We assume that Nexa can reduce the effort required to access services and adapt to individual preferences over time, thereby enhancing user experience.

title: 'I Felt a Sense of Flow': Rendering Spatial Vector Information through Five-Finger Electrotactile Feedback.
abstract: Spatial vector information (SVI), such as force, is ubiquitous in the physical world, yet its rendering in Virtual Reality (VR) remains largely unexplored. This research investigates the use of 3×3 electrotactile arrays attached to the five fingers to render SVI through spatiotemporal asymmetric stimulation. To validate this approach, we conducted a preliminary study examining three aspects: (1) users' subjective intensity perception relative to voltage, (2) differential intensity perception across the five fingers, and (3) direction perception as influenced by scanning frequency on both single and multiple fingers. Results demonstrate a clear linear relationship between perceived intensity and voltage, although significant variations exist among participants and fingers. For direction perception, we observed a general decrease in perceptual clarity with increasing scanning frequency, alongside several distinctive patterns that deviate from this trend. This research offers valuable parametric insights into leveraging electrotactile stimulation for SVI rendering, establishing a foundation for future development of SVI rendering systems in VR.

title: Online Continual Learning for Building Automation on IoT Devices via Coreset Selection.
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled Internet of Things (IoT) devices are crucial in the field of building automation, enabling adaptive and user-centric control of smart environments. In this paper, we propose an online continual learning (OCL) framework based on coreset selection, where IoT cameras capture and analyze human activities, select informative and diverse data subsets, and train neural networks online to replicate user-driven lighting patterns. Our approach combines semantic feature extraction using a CLIP-based vision encoder, temporal modeling with LSTM, and a two-step coreset selection strategy that keeps stability and maximizes diversity. Experimental results on a real-world building automation testbed demonstrate that our method achieves superior adaptability and sustained performance. This work provides a practical solution for robust, adaptive building automation in dynamic, real-world environments.

title: Generating Explanations for Models Predicting Student Exam Performance.
abstract: Understanding and improving student performance is a central concern in education, and predictive models can provide valuable insights—provided their decisions are transparent and explainable. However, many machine learning (ML) models used for this purpose lack interpretability, limiting their practical utility. In this work, we apply two complementary eXplainable AI (XAI) methods: SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and the Bayesian Counterfactual Generator (BayCon), to explain the predictions of an ML model trained on multimodal data to forecast student exam outcomes. SHAP is used to identify and visualise the most influential features contributing to each prediction, while BayCon generates actionable counterfactuals. These counterfactuals are then converted into natural language using a large language model (LLM), making them easier to understand. Our approach is designed to support both students and educators by offering clear, personalised insights into the factors affecting academic performance. We present the explanation generation pipeline and discuss its interpretability and potential benefits for educational contexts.

title: MindfulBreath: Every Breath You Take, Every Mind You Wake.
abstract: Breathing is a common entry point to mindfulness. But for beginners, simply observing the breath can feel vague and hard to follow. We present MindfulBreath, an interactive system that uses real-time respiratory data to recommend a personalized breathing pace and visualize each inhale and exhale as flowing movement through a human figure. Designed as a preparatory experience, MindfulBreath helps users rehearse attentional control and embodied focus before beginning body scan meditation. In a study with 15 participants, Initial findings suggest that MindfulBreath may improve focus, relaxation, and engagement over passive music or standard breathing apps. These preliminary results indicate the potential visually embodied breathing exercises effectively bridge to deeper mindfulness. Unlike conventional mindfulness apps and devices, which offer fixed timing or generic animations, MindfulBreath adapts in real time to each user's unique respiratory pattern, positioning breath not only as a target of observation, but as an accessible medium for embodied mental training.

title: Designing Systems for Long-term Sensemaking.
abstract: Personal informatics systems are widely used for self-tracking but often fall short in supporting long-term sensemaking, or how individuals derive meaningful insights from their data over extended periods of time. Existing tools overlook long-term routine lengths and disruptions and provide short-term feedback for users. This project addresses these limitations by investigating three key factors that inform the design of systems for long-term insights: routine lengths, routine disruptions, and the persistence of user-generated insights. Our investigation of longitudinal sleep records and systems that persist user insights provides key design considerations for supporting long-term sensemaking in personal informatics.

title: A Framework for Modeling User Perceptions to Facilitate Personalized Communication.
abstract: Technology has vastly increased the number of messages we send and receive. Despite the increasing quantity of communication, this digital communication continues to lack many of the nuances of in-person communication. In this work, I discuss my completed and planned work in modeling users' perceptions to facilitate personalized communication using untraditional modalities. I outline the general framework my work uses to develop these systems. I start by collecting participants' perceptions of arbitrary messages, and passively recording the behaviors on which the message will be based. These preferences and behaviors are then combined and communicated to the user. Their perceptions of the message are used to retrain the model to better communicate with the user. Thus far, I have used this framework to develop systems using music to promote physical activity. My planned work intends to validate the framework in a secondary paradigm, wherein a machine studies the users' behavior and adapts to their perceived needs. Overall, this research strives to develop more personalized techniques for communicating with users, striving to improve the impact and clarity of digital communication.

title: FuseLID: Vision-Language Model-Based Camera-Radar Fusion for Liquid Identification.
abstract: Service robots often engage in liquid-related tasks such as pouring, which require accurate liquid identification. Vision-language models (VLM) exhibit strong performance in general object recognition, they struggle to reliably distinguish between visually similar liquids, limiting their effectiveness in such scenarios. As a promising solution, millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar combined with neural networks has been widely adopted for material recognition and liquid identification. However, training a radar-based liquid classifier demands a large volume of labeled radar-liquid data pairs and often faces challenges in generalizing to real-world environments. To address this challenge, we propose FuseLID, a VLM-based camera-radar late-fusion system designed to improve liquid identification performance. FuseLID leverages the weak penetration capability of mmWave signals through liquids and combines this with the robot's precise motion control to capture distinctive radar signatures of various liquids. Subsequently, a VLM-based late-fusion module is designed to combine camera and radar outputs for achieving enhanced liquid identification with limited radar-liquid data. Preliminary experiments show that FuseLID improves liquid identification accuracy from 51.6% to 95.7% when classifying several commonly consumed beverages, including visually similar ones.

title: Thou Shalt Not Prompt: Zero-Shot Human Activity Recognition in Smart Homes via Language Modeling of Sensor Data & Activities.
abstract: Developing zero-shot human activity recognition (HAR) methods is a critical direction in smart home research, considering its impact on making HAR systems work in smart homes that have diverse sensing modalities, layouts, and activities of interest. The state-of-the-art (SOTA) solutions along this direction are based on generating natural language descriptions of sensor data and feeding it via a carefully crafted prompt to the Large Language Models (LLM) for classification. Despite performance guarantees, such ''prompt-the-LLM'' approaches carry several risks, including privacy invasion, reliance on an external service, and inconsistent predictions due to version changes, making a case for alternative zero-shot HAR methods that do not require LLM prompting. In this paper, we propose one such solution that models sensor data and activities using natural language, leveraging its embeddings to perform zero-shot classification and thereby bypassing the need to prompt the LLMs for activity predictions. The impact of our work lies in presenting a detailed case study on six datasets, highlighting how language modeling can bolster HAR systems in zero-shot recognition.

title: Context-Adaptive Hearing Aid Fitting Advisor through Multi-turn Multimodal LLM Conversation.
abstract: Traditional hearing aids often rely on static fittings that fail to adapt to their dynamic acoustic environments. We propose CAFA, a Context-Adaptive Fitting Advisor that provides personalized, real-time hearing aid adjustments through a multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) workflow. CAFA combines live ambient audio, audiograms, and user feedback in a multi-turn conversational system. Ambient sound is classified into conversation, noise, or quiet with 91.2% accuracy using a lightweight neural network based on YAMNet embeddings. This system utilizes a modular LLM workflow, comprising context acquisition, subproblem classification, strategy provision, and ethical regulation, and is overseen by an LLM Judge. The workflow translates context and feedback into precise, safe tuning commands. Evaluation confirms that real-time sound classification enhances conversational efficiency. CAFA exemplifies how agentic, multimodal AI can enable intelligent, user-centric assistive technologies.

title: Poster: Recognizing Hidden-in-the-Ear Private Key for Reliable Silent Speech Interface Using Multi-Task Learning.
abstract: Silent speech interface (SSI) enables hands-free input without audible vocalization, but most SSI systems do not verify speaker identity. We present HEar-ID, which uses consumer active noise-canceling earbuds to capture low-frequency "whisper" audio and high-frequency ultrasonic reflections. Features from both streams pass through a shared encoder, producing embeddings that feed a contrastive branch for user authentication and an SSI head for silent spelling recognition. This design supports decoding of 50 words while reliably rejecting impostors, all on commodity earbuds with a single model. Experiments demonstrate that HEar-ID achieves strong spelling accuracy and robust authentication.

title: TaskWise: Enhancing Cognitive Performance in Task Management through Interactive Detail Enrichment.
abstract: This study introduces TaskWise, an AI-driven to-do list management tool enhancing cognitive performance through interactive detail enrichment. TaskWise addresses the challenge of balancing simplified recording with sufficient initiation context by leveraging Large Language Models for real-time task analysis and proactive detail prompting, supporting effective task initiation and preventing key information omission. A seven-day, six-participant user study showed TaskWise's AI detail inference significantly improved users' task understanding, preparedness, and sense of control. AI-generated prompts served as an effective ''cognitive scaffold,'' aiding memory recall and planning. Users also exhibited significant agency, strategically adopting AI-suggested details based on task context. These findings demonstrate AI's potential to assist task definition and enhance management experience, offering insights for designing future intelligent systems that better support cognitive processes and empower user agency.

title: A Combined Machine Learning and Deep Learning Framework for Transportation Mode Recognition from Smartphone Data.
abstract: Smartphone-based transportation mode recognition enables scalable assessment of mobility behaviors in naturalistic settings. However, classification remains challenging due to sensor noise, contextual confounders, and variability in human movement. Our team, KMET, proposed a multimodal framework that integrates feature-based gradient boosting and deep learning time-series classifiers to distinguish eight locomotion and transportation modes in the Sussex-Huawei Locomotion dataset. Raw sensor data were preprocessed with sensor fusion. Time- and frequency-domain features were extracted for XGBoost, while TimesNet and MLSTM-FCN networks learned representations directly from raw time-series. Transportation mode predictions were aggregated using the HIVE-COTE 2.0. The final model achieved an F1 score equal to 0.957. These findings indicate that combining handcrafted features with deep learning might serve as an ecologically valid and robust transportation mode recognition approach.
